exhibits.title: The Transistor

site.label: Bell Labs, Murray Hill, New Jersey

exhibits.change: A solid-state switch replaced the fragile, hot vacuum tube.
exhibits.context: John Bardeen and Walter Brattain built the point-contact transistor; William Shockley developed the junction transistor. By the late 1950s transistors were shrinking radios and computers.
exhibits.significance: Transistors are the most manufactured human-made objects in history — tens of billions sit on a single modern chip.

exhibits.title: Information Theory
exhibits.change: Information measured in bits, with hard limits on how fast it can be sent.
exhibits.context: Claude Shannon's 'A Mathematical Theory of Communication' defined information mathematically and showed how error-correcting codes could transmit reliably over noisy channels.
exhibits.significance: The mathematics under compression, digital communication and data storage.

exhibits.title: Universal Human Rights
exhibits.change: Nations agreed a common statement of rights belonging to every person.
exhibits.context: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights was drafted by a committee with members from many countries, including Eleanor Roosevelt, P. C. Chang and Charles Malik, and adopted without dissenting votes (with abstentions).
exhibits.significance: A shared reference point for international law and human-rights movements, though applied unevenly.

exhibits.title: Jet Airliners
exhibits.change: Continents a few hours apart.
exhibits.context: The de Havilland Comet entered service in 1952; after fatal accidents revealed metal fatigue, the Boeing 707 and others made jet travel routine from 1958.
exhibits.significance: Global tourism, migration and business — and the fast spread of diseases.

exhibits.title: The Double Helix
exhibits.change: The molecule of heredity was a code written in four letters.
exhibits.context: James Watson and Francis Crick proposed the double-helix structure of DNA, using X-ray diffraction data from Rosalind Franklin and Maurice Wilkins. Franklin's crucial contribution was long underacknowledged.
exhibits.significance: Molecular biology, genetic medicine, DNA forensics and the reading of ancient genomes all follow.

exhibits.title: The Silicon Solar Cell
exhibits.change: Sunlight turned directly into useful electricity.
exhibits.context: Daryl Chapin, Calvin Fuller and Gerald Pearson made the first practical silicon photovoltaic cell. Early uses included satellites; costs fell dramatically in the 21st century.
exhibits.significance: Now among the cheapest sources of new electricity in much of the world.

exhibits.title: Nuclear Power
exhibits.change: Electricity from atomic fission fed a public grid.
exhibits.context: The Obninsk reactor was the first connected to a grid; Calder Hall in England was the first commercial-scale station. Accidents at Three Mile Island (1979), Chernobyl (1986) and Fukushima (2011) shaped public attitudes.
exhibits.significance: Large-scale low-carbon electricity, with debated risks and waste challenges.

exhibits.title: Polio Vaccine
exhibits.change: A feared childhood disease became preventable.
exhibits.context: Jonas Salk's injected vaccine was declared safe and effective in 1955 after a huge field trial; Albert Sabin's oral vaccine followed. Wild poliovirus now persists in very few places.
exhibits.significance: Mass vaccination as a global public-health tool.

exhibits.title: The Shipping Container
exhibits.change: A standard steel box moved goods from factory to ship to truck unopened.
exhibits.context: Malcolm McLean's first container ship sailed in 1956. ISO standardisation let any port handle any container, and shipping costs fell drastically.
exhibits.significance: The quiet enabler of globalised manufacturing.

exhibits.title: The Space Age
exhibits.change: A human-made object circled the Earth.
exhibits.context: The Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1, a 58 cm sphere whose radio beeps were heard worldwide. The shock accelerated a space race: the first satellites, humans in orbit, and the Moon within twelve years.
exhibits.significance: Humanity left the planet. Satellites now carry weather forecasting, navigation, communication and much of our knowledge of Earth's climate.

exhibits.title: The Integrated Circuit
exhibits.change: A whole circuit made in one piece of semiconductor.
exhibits.context: Jack Kilby built the first integrated circuit on germanium; Robert Noyce independently devised the planar silicon chip that could be mass-produced. The number of transistors per chip then doubled roughly every two years for decades.
exhibits.significance: Cheap, ever-more-powerful electronics — the compounding engine of the digital age.

exhibits.title: The Laser

regions.note: Basov and Prokhorov's maser and laser theory.

exhibits.change: Light in perfect step: a beam of one colour and direction.
exhibits.context: Theodore Maiman built the first working laser with a ruby crystal, based on stimulated emission predicted by Einstein in 1917 and on maser work in the US and USSR.
exhibits.significance: Fibre-optic internet, surgery, barcode scanners, manufacturing and gravitational-wave detectors.

exhibits.title: A Human in Orbit
exhibits.change: Yuri Gagarin circled the Earth once and came home.
exhibits.context: Vostok 1's flight lasted 108 minutes. Valentina Tereshkova became the first woman in space in 1963.
exhibits.significance: Humans could survive and work beyond the atmosphere.

exhibits.title: Video Games
exhibits.change: Computers became something to play.
exhibits.context: Spacewar!, written on a PDP-1 at MIT, spread to research computers across the US. Arcade games and the Magnavox Odyssey (1972) brought games to the public; Japanese companies soon led the industry.
exhibits.significance: A new medium and art form — and the industry that drove consumer graphics and parallel computing.

exhibits.title: Plate Tectonics
exhibits.change: Continents ride on moving plates.
exhibits.context: Wegener's continental drift was widely rejected until seafloor mapping, magnetic stripes and earthquake data in the 1960s showed plates spreading and sinking.
exhibits.significance: Explains earthquakes, volcanoes, mountains — and why fossils of the same animals lie on separated continents.

exhibits.title: The Green Revolution
exhibits.change: New dwarf varieties, fertiliser and irrigation doubled and tripled grain yields.
exhibits.context: Plant breeders including Norman Borlaug developed short-stemmed, high-yield wheat and rice that could use synthetic fertiliser. Famine predictions for South Asia did not come to pass. Critics point to water depletion, pesticide use, loss of crop diversity and unequal benefits.
exhibits.significance: World food production outpaced a doubling population.

exhibits.title: Optical Fibre

regions.note: Charles Kao at Standard Telecommunication Laboratories.

exhibits.change: Light pulses in hair-thin glass carry vast amounts of data.
exhibits.context: Charles Kao showed that purified glass could carry light over long distances; Corning made low-loss fibre in 1970. Undersea fibre cables now carry nearly all intercontinental internet traffic.
exhibits.significance: The physical backbone of the internet.

exhibits.title: The Graphical Interface

site.label: Menlo Park and Palo Alto, California

exhibits.change: Windows, a mouse and pointing — computers for everyone.
exhibits.context: Douglas Engelbart's 1968 demonstration showed the mouse, hypertext and video conferencing. Xerox PARC's Alto developed windows and icons; Apple and later Microsoft brought them to mass markets.
exhibits.significance: Made computing accessible without learning commands.

exhibits.title: ARPANET

regions.note: Donald Davies developed packet switching independently (NPL).

exhibits.change: Computers exchanged data in packets across a network.
exhibits.context: Paul Baran and Donald Davies independently conceived packet switching. ARPANET's first message crashed after two letters ('LO'). The network grew to link universities and research labs.
exhibits.significance: The direct ancestor of the internet.

exhibits.title: Footsteps on the Moon

regions.note: Watched live by hundreds of millions worldwide.

exhibits.change: People walked on another world.
exhibits.context: Apollo 11's Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin landed while Michael Collins orbited. Twelve astronauts walked on the Moon between 1969 and 1972. The program's guidance computer and software, led in part by Margaret Hamilton's team, were landmarks of their own.
exhibits.significance: A 66-year arc from Kitty Hawk to the Moon — and the famous images of Earth from space.

exhibits.title: The Microprocessor

regions.note: Designed with Busicom engineers, including Masatoshi Shima.

exhibits.change: A whole computer processor on one chip.
exhibits.context: The Intel 4004, designed by Federico Faggin, Ted Hoff, Stanley Mazor and Masatoshi Shima, had about 2,300 transistors.
exhibits.significance: Computers could now be put inside anything.

exhibits.title: The Mobile Phone
exhibits.change: A telephone you could carry in your hand.
exhibits.context: Martin Cooper of Motorola made the first handheld cellular call. NTT launched the first commercial cellular network in Tokyo in 1979; Nordic countries followed in 1981.
exhibits.significance: Mobile phones reached billions, often skipping landlines entirely.

exhibits.title: The Personal Computer
exhibits.change: A computer of your own, on your desk.
exhibits.context: Hobbyist kits became consumer products; spreadsheets and word processors made them indispensable in offices. Home computers spread widely in Europe, Japan and beyond.
exhibits.significance: Computing moved from institutions to individuals.

exhibits.title: Voyager
exhibits.change: Two probes toured the outer planets and left the Sun's bubble.
exhibits.context: Voyager 1 and 2 flew past Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. Voyager 1 entered interstellar space in 2012 and carries a golden record of sounds and images from Earth.
exhibits.significance: The farthest human-made objects, still sending data.

exhibits.title: In Vitro Fertilisation
exhibits.change: A child conceived outside the body.
exhibits.context: Robert Edwards, Patrick Steptoe and Jean Purdy achieved the first IVF birth. Millions of children have since been born through assisted reproduction.
exhibits.significance: Transformed fertility medicine.

exhibits.title: Satellite Navigation
exhibits.change: Anyone, anywhere, could know where they are to within metres.
exhibits.context: GPS works by timing signals from atomic clocks in orbit — it must correct for both special and general relativity. Opened for civilian use, it now underpins transport, farming, finance and phones.
exhibits.significance: Position and time as a free global utility.

exhibits.title: Smallpox Eradicated
exhibits.change: A disease that killed hundreds of millions was wiped out.
exhibits.context: The WHO's intensified campaign from 1967 used surveillance and ring vaccination, with health workers in dozens of countries. The last natural case was Ali Maow Maalin in Somalia in 1977.
exhibits.significance: The only human disease eradicated so far — proof of what global cooperation can do.

exhibits.title: The Internet

regions.note: The French CYCLADES network influenced its design.

exhibits.change: Separate computer networks joined into one network of networks.
exhibits.context: TCP/IP let different networks exchange packets with no central control; ARPANET switched over on 1 January 1983. Commercial providers, email and, from 1991, the World Wide Web opened it to the public.
exhibits.significance: A single global system for sharing knowledge — the most connected moment of the story this Museum tells.
